imo-1989-01.title: Equal-sum triples plus snake-ordered blocks
imo-1989-01.body:
Note $1989=117\cdot17$. Let $m=117$, $h=\frac{m-1}2=58$, and index the sets by $j=0,1,\dots,116$.

**Step 1: $117$ triples from $\{1,\dots,351\}$ with equal sums.** For $j=0,\dots,m-1$ let
$$x_j=j,\qquad y_j=(j+h)\bmod m,\qquad z_j=3h-x_j-y_j .$$
$x_j$ and $y_j$ each run through $0,\dots,m-1$. The sums $x_j+y_j$ are: for $0\le j\le h$, $y_j=j+h$ and $x_j+y_j=2j+h\in\{h,h+2,\dots,3h\}$; for $h+1\le j\le 2h$, $y_j=j+h-m$ and $x_j+y_j=2j-h-1\in\{h+1,h+3,\dots,3h-1\}$. Together these are exactly the $m$ consecutive integers $h,h+1,\dots,3h$, each once, so $z_j=3h-(x_j+y_j)$ also runs through $0,\dots,2h=m-1$. Put into $A_j$ the three numbers
$$x_j+1\in\{1..117\},\qquad y_j+118\in\{118..234\},\qquad z_j+235\in\{235..351\};$$
they use each of $1,\dots,351$ exactly once, and each triple has sum $3h+354$.

**Step 2: the remaining $1638=14\cdot117$ numbers.** Split $352,\dots,1989$ into $14$ blocks of $117$ consecutive numbers: block $t$ ($t=0,\dots,13$) is $\{352+117t,\dots,352+117t+116\}$. Put into $A_j$ the number $352+117t+j$ if $t$ is even and $352+117t+116-j$ if $t$ is odd. For each pair of blocks $t=2u,2u+1$, set $A_j$ receives
$$(352+117\cdot2u+j)+(352+117(2u+1)+116-j),$$
which does not depend on $j$.

So each $A_j$ gets $3+14=17$ numbers, all of $1,\dots,1989$ are used exactly once, and all sets have the same sum (namely $\frac{1989\cdot1990}{2\cdot117}=16915$). ∎

imo-1989-02.title: Excentral triangle and the incentre–excentre lemma
imo-1989-02.body:
Let $I$ be the incentre and write $A,B,C$ also for the angles; $[\cdot]$ is area. The internal bisector of $A$ and the external bisectors of $B$ and $C$ meet at the excentre opposite $A$, so $A_0,B_0,C_0$ are the three excentres. Internal and external bisectors at a vertex are perpendicular, so $B_0,A,C_0$ are collinear on the external bisector at $A$ and $A_0A\perp B_0C_0$; similarly for $B$ and $C$. Thus $A,B,C$ are the feet of the altitudes of triangle $A_0B_0C_0$, and $I$ (the common point of $AA_0,BB_0,CC_0$) is its orthocentre. Its angle at $A_0$ is $\angle BA_0C$ (as $B\in A_0C_0$, $C\in A_0B_0$); in the quadrilateral $A_0BIC$ the angles at $B$ and $C$ are right, so $\angle BA_0C=180^\circ-\angle BIC=180^\circ-(90^\circ+\frac A2)=90^\circ-\frac A2$. So triangle $A_0B_0C_0$ is acute.

**Lemma: $A_1$ is the midpoint of $IA_0$.** $\angle A_1BI=\angle A_1BC+\angle CBI=\angle A_1AC+\frac B2=\frac A2+\frac B2$, and $\angle A_1IB=\angle IAB+\angle IBA=\frac A2+\frac B2$ (exterior angle of triangle $ABI$). So $A_1B=A_1I$. Since $\angle IBA_0=90^\circ$, we get $\angle A_1BA_0=90^\circ-\angle A_1BI=90^\circ-\angle A_1IB=\angle A_1A_0B$, so also $A_1B=A_1A_0$. As $A_1$ lies on segment $IA_0$ (on ray $AI$, $I$ is inside the circumcircle, $A_1$ on it and $A_0$ outside it), $A_1$ is the midpoint of $IA_0$. Similarly $B_1$, $C_1$ are the midpoints of $IB_0$, $IC_0$.

**(i)** The boundary of triangle $A_0B_0C_0$ passes through $A_0,C,B_0,A,C_0,B$ in this order, and $I$ is inside it, so
$$[A_0B_0C_0]=[IA_0C]+[ICB_0]+[IB_0A]+[IAC_0]+[IC_0B]+[IBA_0].$$
Because $A_1$ is the midpoint of $IA_0$, $[IA_0C]=2[IA_1C]$ and $[IBA_0]=2[IBA_1]$; similarly for the others. Hence
$$[A_0B_0C_0]=2\big([IA_1C]+[ICB_1]+[IB_1A]+[IAC_1]+[IC_1B]+[IBA_1]\big).$$
The points $A,C_1,B,A_1,C,B_1$ lie on the circumcircle in this order ($C_1$ is the midpoint of arc $AB$ not containing $C$, etc.), so the hexagon $AC_1BA_1CB_1$ is convex, and $I$ (inside triangle $ABC$) lies inside it; the six triangles in the bracket tile the hexagon. So $[A_0B_0C_0]=2[AC_1BA_1CB_1]$.

**(ii)** Let $\alpha_0,\beta_0,\gamma_0$ be the (acute) angles of $A_0B_0C_0$ at $A_0,B_0,C_0$. Since $B$ is the foot of the altitude from $B_0$, which lies on line $A_0C_0$, the right triangle $B_0BA_0$ gives $A_0B=A_0B_0\cos\alpha_0$; similarly $A_0C=A_0C_0\cos\alpha_0$. Hence
$$[A_0BC]=\tfrac12A_0B\cdot A_0C\sin\alpha_0=\cos^2\alpha_0\,[A_0B_0C_0],$$
and similarly at $B_0$, $C_0$. The triangle $A_0B_0C_0$ is split into $ABC$ and these three corner triangles, so
$$[ABC]=[A_0B_0C_0]\big(1-\cos^2\alpha_0-\cos^2\beta_0-\cos^2\gamma_0\big).$$
Finally, for angles $X+Y+Z=180^\circ$,
$$\cos^2X+\cos^2Y=1+\tfrac12(\cos2X+\cos2Y)=1+\cos(X+Y)\cos(X-Y)=1-\cos Z\cos(X-Y),$$
so
$$\cos^2X+\cos^2Y+\cos^2Z\ge1-|\cos Z|+\cos^2Z=\tfrac34+\big(|\cos Z|-\tfrac12\big)^2\ge\tfrac34 .$$
Therefore $[ABC]\le\frac14[A_0B_0C_0]$, i.e. $[A_0B_0C_0]\ge4[ABC]$ (equality for the equilateral triangle). ∎

imo-1989-03.title: Double count isosceles triangles
imo-1989-03.body:
For each $P\in S$ choose a set $C_P$ of exactly $k$ points of $S$ all at the same distance from $P$ (possible by (ii)). Count the pairs $\big(P,\{Q,R\}\big)$ with $P\in S$ and $\{Q,R\}\subseteq C_P$, $Q\ne R$.

**By $P$:** exactly $n\binom k2$ pairs.

**By $\{Q,R\}$:** if $\{Q,R\}\subseteq C_P$ then $PQ=PR$, so $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $QR$. By (i) a line contains at most $2$ points of $S$, so each of the $\binom n2$ pairs $\{Q,R\}$ is counted at most twice.

Hence $n\binom k2\le2\binom n2$, i.e. $k(k-1)\le2(n-1)$, so $k^2-k-(2n-2)\le0$ and
$$k\le\frac{1+\sqrt{1+8(n-1)}}2=\frac12+\sqrt{2n-\tfrac74}<\frac12+\sqrt{2n}.$$
∎

imo-1989-04.title: Angles at $P$ in the rigid triangle $ABP$
imo-1989-04.body:
Let $a=AD$, $b=BC$, so $AB=a+b$, $AP=a+h$, $BP=b+h$: the triangle $ABP$ is determined by $a,b,h$. (Geometrically, the circles with centres $A,B,P$ and radii $a,b,h$ are pairwise externally tangent, and the circle around $P$ touches line $CD$.) Let $\ell$ be line $CD$ and $\mathbf n$ the unit normal of $\ell$ pointing into the half-plane containing the quadrilateral. For a point $X$ let $\operatorname{ht}(X)$ be its signed distance from $\ell$ (positive on that side). Then $\operatorname{ht}(P)=h$, $\operatorname{ht}(C)=\operatorname{ht}(D)=0$, and since $D,C\in\ell$,
$$0<\operatorname{ht}(A)\le AD=a,\qquad 0<\operatorname{ht}(B)\le BC=b .$$

**Step 1: the ray from $P$ in direction $\mathbf n$ leaves the quadrilateral through side $AB$.** It leaves the convex quadrilateral at a boundary point $X$ with $\operatorname{ht}(X)=h+PX>0$, so $X\notin CD$. Suppose $X$ lies on side $BC$, $X\ne B$. Heights are linear along $BC$, so $\operatorname{ht}(X)=\frac{XC}{b}\operatorname{ht}(B)\le XC=b-BX$. Thus $h+PX\le b-BX$, i.e. $BX+XP\le b-h$; but $BX+XP\ge BP=b+h$ — a contradiction. In the same way $X$ is not on side $DA$ except at $A$. Hence $X$ lies on the closed segment $AB$, and the ray $PX$ lies inside angle $APB$:
$$\varphi_A+\varphi_B=\theta,\qquad\varphi_A=\angle APX,\ \varphi_B=\angle XPB,\ \theta=\angle APB .$$

**Step 2: lower bounds for $\varphi_A,\varphi_B$.** $\operatorname{ht}(A)=h+(a+h)\cos\varphi_A\le a$, so $\cos\varphi_A\le\frac{a-h}{a+h}=\cos\alpha$ for the angle $\alpha\in(0,\pi)$ with this cosine; hence $\varphi_A\ge\alpha$. Likewise $\varphi_B\ge\beta$ with $\cos\beta=\frac{b-h}{b+h}$. So $\theta\ge\alpha+\beta$. Using $\tan^2\frac x2=\frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}$:
$$\tan^2\frac\alpha2=\frac ha,\qquad\tan^2\frac\beta2=\frac hb,$$
and from the law of cosines in triangle $ABP$, $1-\cos\theta=\frac{4ab}{2(a+h)(b+h)}$, $1+\cos\theta=\frac{4h(a+b+h)}{2(a+h)(b+h)}$, so
$$\tan^2\frac\theta2=\frac{ab}{h(a+b+h)} .$$

**Step 3: algebra.** Put $u=\frac1{\sqrt a}$, $v=\frac1{\sqrt b}$; we must show $h(u+v)^2\le1$. Since $\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\le\frac\theta2<\frac\pi2$ and $\tan$ is increasing there, with $\tan\frac\alpha2\tan\frac\beta2=huv<1$:
$$\tan\frac\theta2\ge\tan\frac{\alpha+\beta}2=\frac{\sqrt h\,(u+v)}{1-huv}.$$
Also $\tan^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1}{h\,Q}$ with $Q=\frac{a+b+h}{ab}=u^2+v^2+hu^2v^2$. So
$$1-huv\ge h(u+v)\sqrt Q. \tag{$*$}$$
Suppose $h(u+v)^2>1$. Then
$$h^2(u+v)^2Q=h^2(u+v)^2(u^2+v^2)+h^3(u+v)^2u^2v^2>h(u^2+v^2)+h^2u^2v^2,$$
and $h(u^2+v^2)+h^2u^2v^2-(1-huv)^2=h(u+v)^2-1>0$. So $h(u+v)\sqrt Q>1-huv>0$, contradicting $(*)$. Hence $h(u+v)^2\le1$, i.e.
$$\frac1{\sqrt h}\ge\frac1{\sqrt{AD}}+\frac1{\sqrt{BC}}.$$
(Equality holds when $CD$ is tangent to all three circles.) ∎

imo-1989-05.title: Chinese remainder theorem
imo-1989-05.body:
Choose $2n$ distinct primes $p_1,q_1,p_2,q_2,\dots,p_n,q_n$. The moduli $p_1q_1,\dots,p_nq_n$ are pairwise coprime, so by the Chinese remainder theorem there is a positive integer $x$ with
$$x\equiv-i\pmod{p_iq_i}\qquad(i=1,\dots,n).$$
Then $x+i$ is divisible by the two different primes $p_i$ and $q_i$, so it is not a power of a single prime (and it is $>1$, so it is not $p^0=1$ either). Thus $x+1,\dots,x+n$ work. ∎

imo-1989-05.title: Explicit numbers with factorials
imo-1989-05.body:
Let $N=(n+1)!$ and consider $N^2+k$ for $k=2,3,\dots,n+1$. Suppose $N^2+k=p^e$ for a prime $p$. Since $k\mid N$, we get $k\mid N^2+k$, so $k=p^j$ with $j\ge1$ (as $k\ge2$) and
$$\frac{N^2}{k}+1=p^{e-j}.$$
Now $\frac{N^2}{k}=N\cdot\frac Nk$ is divisible by $p$ (because $p\mid k\mid N$), so the left side is $\equiv1\pmod p$; hence $p^{e-j}=1$ and $\frac{N^2}k=0$, absurd. So the $n$ consecutive numbers $N^2+2,\dots,N^2+n+1$ contain no prime power. ∎

imo-1989-06.title: An injection that is not onto
imo-1989-06.body:
Call $a$ and $a\pm n$ *partners*; each number in $\{1,\dots,2n\}$ has exactly one partner. Property $P$ means some two partners are adjacent. Let $\mathcal A$ be the set of permutations with property $P$ and $\mathcal B$ those without.

**The map.** Let $\sigma=(x_1,\dots,x_{2n})\in\mathcal B$ and let $x_k$ be the partner of $x_1$; then $k\ge3$ (as $x_1,x_2$ are not partners). Define
$$\phi(\sigma)=(x_2,\dots,x_{k-1},x_1,x_k,\dots,x_{2n}),$$
i.e. move $x_1$ to the place just before its partner. In $\phi(\sigma)$ the pair $x_1,x_k$ is adjacent, at positions $k-1,k$ with $k-1\ge2$. All other adjacent pairs were adjacent in $\sigma$ (hence not partners), except $x_{k-1},x_1$, which are not partners since the only partner of $x_1$ is $x_k$. So $\phi(\sigma)\in\mathcal A$, and it has **exactly one** adjacent pair of partners, not at positions $1,2$.

**Injective.** From $\tau=\phi(\sigma)$ we recover $\sigma$: find the unique adjacent pair of partners in $\tau$ and move its first element to the front.

**Not onto.** A permutation whose first two entries are partners, e.g. $(1,n+1,2,3,\dots,n,n+2,\dots,2n)$, is in $\mathcal A$ but not in the image of $\phi$ (images have their only partner pair at positions $\ge2$).

Hence $|\mathcal B|<|\mathcal A|$. ∎
